article_title: AWS Continuum Reaches GA With Per-Line, Per-Inference Pricing; Google's CodeMender, Not AWS's Tool, Runs the Behavior-Equivalence Check
summary: Automated checks pass, but manual review overrides to REJECT: the Analysis fails the policy's independent-sourcing requirement, and the one paragraph carrying the article's central comparative claim contains three misquotes of its source.

findings.message: Analysis independent-sourcing requirement not met: only 1 of 6 cited sources is independent of the subjects compared, not the 2 required by config/editorial_policy.md 'Analysis requirements'.
findings.details: Policy: 'at least 2 [sources] are independent of the subject (not the vendor's, project's or organisation's own release notes, blog, changelog or documentation)... Independence is counted by outlet: several articles from one outlet... are a single source.' This Analysis is explicitly a head-to-head comparison of AWS Continuum and Google CodeMender (the headline names both), so both are subjects of the piece, not just AWS. Of the 6 cited URLs: the two InfoQ articles are one outlet and count as a single independent source; the three AWS pages (docs x2 + pricing) are AWS's own documentation/vendor material, excluded by the policy's parenthetical; and the DeepMind CodeMender blog is Google's own blog about its own product -- also excluded by the same parenthetical, since CodeMender is a co-subject of the comparison, not incidental background. The article itself concedes this: 'DeepMind's regression-testing claims and AWS's patch-delivery mechanics come from each company's own materials, not from an outside audit of either tool's real-world error rate.' That sentence is an accurate admission that neither side of the comparison has independent verification -- which means the count of independent sources is 1 (InfoQ), not the 2 the writer's self-report claimed (two InfoQ articles treated as separate sources, plus the DeepMind blog treated as independent). An article labelled Analysis that does not meet the 2-independent-source bar is not an Analysis, and the submission's category field is part of the signed payload and cannot be edited to recategorize it as News or Briefing without breaking the signature.

findings.message: Three direct quotations attributed to Google DeepMind's CodeMender blog are paraphrases presented inside quote marks, not verbatim source text.
findings.details: All three appear in the 'Implications' section, in the paragraph carrying the article's central comparative claim. (1) Article quotes: "an LLM-based critique tool that highlights differences between original and modified code to detect regressions". Source (deepmind.google, source-5.html.gz) actually reads: "CodeMender uses a large language model-based critique tool that highlights the differences between the original and modified code in order to verify that the proposed changes do not introduce regressions, and self-correct as needed." The quoted fragment compresses and rewords the source rather than reproducing it. (2) Article quotes: "differential testing, fuzzing, and SMT solvers for systematic code scrutiny". Source actually reads: "We developed tools based on advanced program analysis that include static analysis, dynamic analysis, differential testing, fuzzing and SMT solvers. Using these tools to systematically scrutinize code patterns, control flow and data flow, CodeMender can better identify the root causes of security flaws and architectural weaknesses." The quoted fragment drops 'static analysis, dynamic analysis' from the tool list and compresses an entire second sentence into 'for systematic code scrutiny.' (3) Article quotes: "currently, all CodeMender-generated patches undergo human researcher review before upstream submission". Source actually reads: "Currently, all patches generated by CodeMender are reviewed by human researchers before they're submitted upstream." None of the three paraphrases materially changes the underlying fact (the critique tool does flag regressions, the tool list does include the named techniques, and the human-review requirement is accurately restated), but presenting a paraphrase inside quotation marks as if verbatim is a quote-fidelity violation regardless of whether the substance holds.

findings.message: The $18,200 context-fee figure was independently recomputed from AWS's own tier table and matches both the article's claim and AWS's own published worked example.
findings.details: AWS's pricing page (source-3.html.gz) lists: 'First 10 million $200 / Next 90 million $180 / Above 100 million through 1 billion $160 / Above 1 billion through 10 billion $130 / Above 10 billion $100' per million lines/month, and a $10/CIU inference fee. Recomputing for 100 million lines: 10M x $200/1M = $2,000, plus 90M x $180/1M = $16,200, totaling $18,200. This matches both the article's claim and AWS's own 'Example 3: Enterprise codebase' on the same page, which states verbatim: 'Context fee: $200 per 1 million for the first 10 million ($2,000) plus $180 per 1 million for the next 90 million ($16,200) = $18,200... Inference fee: 10,000 vulnerabilities x 2 units x $10 per unit = $200,000... Estimated monthly total: $218,200.' InfoQ's November article (source-0.html.gz) independently arrives at the same $18,200/$200,000/$218,200/'$20 per validated finding' breakdown. All four figures in the article ($18,200, $200,000, $218,200, ~$20/finding) check out exactly against both the AWS primary source and the InfoQ secondary source.

findings.message: The central comparative claim (AWS Continuum's documented delivery path lacks an automated behavior-equivalence check that Google's CodeMender has) is accurately sourced and appropriately scoped, not an absence-claim overreach.
findings.details: AWS's own documentation pages fetched for this submission (what-is-continuum.html and cv-viewing-patches.html) describe only a human-review step ('Review generated patches to understand the proposed code changes before you apply them') and an opt-in auto-delivery setting ('Automatically deliver remediation patches') that does not require that review as a precondition. Neither page, nor the AWS pricing page, mentions any automated regression or behavior-equivalence check. The article's claim is carefully scoped to 'AWS Continuum's documented delivery path' (the two docs pages actually fetched), not to a blanket claim that AWS has no such capability anywhere. InfoQ's November article independently corroborates the substance: discussing CodeMender's 'LLM-as-a-judge framework that tests for program equivalence,' it states 'That is the step AWS's console caveat concedes Continuum does not perform.' Checked against both the AWS primary source and an independent outlet, not just the source adjacent to the claim, per the absence-claim test in editorial policy.

content_preview.title: AWS Continuum Reaches GA With Per-Line, Per-Inference Pricing; Google's CodeMender, Not AWS's Tool, Runs the Behavior-Equivalence Check
content_preview.summary: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now GA with usage-based pricing; sources show it and Google's CodeMender draw the autonomous-patch trust line differently.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Amazon Web Services has taken Continuum for code vulnerabilities out of gated preview and into general availability, in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon), according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/11/aws-continuum-ga/). The service prices its work by the line of code it watches and by the number of validation steps it runs, and it already offers to open pull requests or upload patch files on a customer's behalf. Google's competing tool, CodeMender, takes a narrow...

recommendations: Resubmit as a new submission (not a rewrite of this one, per the v3.9.0 no-rewrite policy): either add at least one more source that is independent of both AWS and Google (a third-party security researcher, an analyst note, or outside commentary on CodeMender's actual patch quality) to legitimately clear the 2-independent-source Analysis bar, or recategorize the piece as News/Briefing if the independent-sourcing bar can't be cleared.

If resubmitted with the DeepMind blog as a source, quote it verbatim and in full for any claim placed inside quotation marks; the three paraphrases found here (critique-tool description, program-analysis tool list, human-review statement) are each easy to fix by copying the source's exact wording.

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear structure (Overview/Background/Current Situation/Implications), appropriate technical depth for a DevSecOps audience, facts and analysis are visibly separated (the Implications section explicitly flags what is reported vs. what follows from comparing reports). Prose quality is not the problem with this submission.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 6 sources read from their gzipped snapshots on disk (source-0 through source-5 in sources/2026-11/aws-continuum-reaches-ga-with-per-line-per-inference-pricing-googles-codemender-not-awss-tool-runs-the-behavior-equivalence-check/), all with status_code 200, all sha256-verified against manifest.json, none flagged with suspicious_patterns. source-0 (InfoQ, Nov 6 2026, 'AWS Ships Continuum for Code Vulnerabilities') confirmed verbatim: 'an optional collector supplying resource and network context from wherever the code runs,' 'Continuum confirms which findings are reachable by running the exploit in an isolated sandbox,' 'a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone,' 'most becomes noise that doesn't matter in your environment' (Rae), 'leads AI security go-to-market' (Rae's title), and the $18,200/$200,000/$218,200/~$20-per-finding pricing breakdown. source-1 (InfoQ, Jul 16 2026) confirmed verbatim: 'Continuum is built on lessons learned from running security across AWS and Amazon.com' (Kapoor, correctly titled VP of search, security, and observability), 'already generally available with established pricing,' 'in preview,' 'in gated preview.' source-2 (AWS Continuum user guide, what-is-continuum.html) confirmed verbatim: 'Frontier AI models have given attackers new capabilities, such as generating complex exploits from vulnerability disclosures in minutes rather than hours,' 'integrates with GitHub and Amazon S3 for code and context,' and confirmed penetration testing/threat modeling are documented under a separate AWS Security Agent User Guide. source-3 (AWS Continuum pricing page) confirmed the full tier table (First 10M $200 / Next 90M $180 / 100M-1B $160 / 1B-10B $130 / above 10B $100), the $10/CIU inference rate, the $50/task-hour penetration-testing rate, and AWS's own 'Example 3' worked example producing $18,200 context fee / $200,000 inference fee / $218,200 total -- independently recomputed and confirmed correct (see findings). source-4 (AWS Continuum docs, cv-viewing-patches.html) confirmed verbatim: 'Review generated patches to understand the proposed code changes before you apply them,' 'Automatically deliver remediation patches,' 'For GitHub, AWS Continuum creates pull requests. For Amazon S3, AWS Continuum uploads patch files under continuum-patches/ in your bucket' -- and confirmed this page describes no automated behavior-equivalence or regression check, only the opt-in automatic-delivery setting and a request to review before applying. source-5 (Google DeepMind CodeMender blog, dated October 6, 2025) confirmed '72 security fixes,' 'as large as 4.5 million lines of code,' and the CVE-2023-4863/libwebp reference as accurate, but found three quotations in this paragraph that are paraphrases, not verbatim source text (see findings) -- this is the one source with a quote-fidelity problem. Also note for the record: the DeepMind blog is dated October 6, 2025, meaning the '72 security fixes... over six months' figure is roughly 13 months old as of this November 2026 submission; the article doesn't date the figure, which risks reading as more current than it is, though it does not misstate what DeepMind said. Allowlist: infoq.com, aws.amazon.com, docs.aws.amazon.com and deepmind.google are all already present in config/source_allowlist.txt; no allowlist additions needed. Anthropic disclosure: not required - Anthropic is not a subject of this article and is not named in the headline, summary, or lead.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every specific fact checked against its source (GA regions, pricing tiers, context/inference fee structure, CodeMender's patch count and codebase size, the CVE reference, the human-review requirement, the penetration-testing rate) traces correctly to the cited source. The $18,200 figure was independently recomputed from AWS's raw tier table rather than taken on trust, and matches both AWS's own worked example and InfoQ's independent calculation. The absence claim at the article's core (AWS's documented delivery path has no equivalent to CodeMender's automated equivalence check) was checked against the actual AWS documentation pages fetched, not just inferred from the InfoQ framing, and is accurately scoped to 'documented delivery path' rather than overclaimed as a blanket absence. The accuracy problem is narrower: three quotations in the CodeMender paragraph are paraphrases dressed as verbatim quotes (see findings) -- none of them changes the underlying fact, but all three fail the 'quote marks mean verbatim' rule.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and analytical throughout; no sensationalism, no editorializing beyond what the Implications section explicitly frames as inference from the reported facts. No AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: Genuinely new topic -- no existing article in src/content/articles/ covers AWS Continuum or CodeMender; checked both by filename grep and content grep across the archive.
concerns: Analysis requirement: only 1 of 6 sources is independent of the two subjects being compared (AWS and Google), not the 2 required by editorial policy for an Analysis. The article's own text ('each company's own materials, not from an outside audit') concedes exactly this.
Three quotations attributed to the DeepMind CodeMender blog, in the paragraph that carries the article's central comparative claim, are paraphrases rather than verbatim source text.
The DeepMind blog's '72 security fixes... over six months' figure is from an October 2025 post and is about 13 months stale relative to this November 2026 submission; the article does not date it.
recommendations: A new submission on this topic should add at least one source independent of both AWS and Google, or be submitted as News/Briefing instead of Analysis.
Quote the DeepMind blog verbatim wherever quotation marks are used.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: REJECT. Automated checks pass and the reported facts are accurate and well-sourced for what they are, but this submission does not meet the Analysis format it claims: only one of six sources (InfoQ, counted once by outlet) is independent of the two companies being compared, short of the policy's 2-independent-source bar, and the article's category field is part of the signed submission and cannot be edited to recategorize it. That structural gap is compounded, not offset, by three paraphrased-as-verbatim quotations in the single paragraph that carries the article's central comparative claim (CodeMender's own blog description of its validation pipeline and human-review policy). Neither issue is a single, isolated slip that a corrections note can honestly absorb while leaving the Analysis label and its implied sourcing standard intact. The underlying story -- AWS Continuum's GA pricing and its narrower, less independently-verified safety posture versus CodeMender -- is sound and worth another pass with proper sourcing. Featured candidacy: 1 - solid, accurate story of interest to a defined DevSecOps/cloud-security audience, contingent on the sourcing and quote-fidelity issues being fixed in a future submission; not scored higher because the comparison itself cannot currently be sourced from outside either vendor's own account of itself.
